canberra.title: Braidwood’s first Big Wheels Festival promises a truckload of family fun
canberra.snippet: If you’re a fan of big trucks and lots of them, then come 10 October you’ll need to make tracks to Braidwood, where the first-ever Braidw...
canberra.content:
The Braidwood Big Wheels Festival will be a celebration of trucks both old and new. Photo: Braidwood Big Wheels Festival.

If you’re a fan of big trucks and lots of them, then come 10 October you’ll need to make tracks to Braidwood, where the first-ever Braidwood Big Wheels Festival will be taking place.

The community-focused event will be the first of its kind in Braidwood, and the organising committee, made up of members of the Braidwood Lion’s Club, hopes people from across the region will turn out in full force.

The idea for a truck-centric fundraiser was hatched by local truck driver and Braidwood Freight owner Nick Turner, who is looking forward to delivering a full day of family fun.

The restored Gellibrand cared for by the Braidwoood Museum and Heritage Centre will be taking part in the festival. Photo: Braidwood Museum.

The event will begin on Braidwood’s main street, where more than 60 trucks, tractors and heritage vehicles will form a convoy before making their way to the local showground, where the festivities are set to continue throughout the day.

“What we want to achieve is a great family day out. All proceeds raised will go back into community initiatives run by Lions in the region. We have programs that support young people in conjunction with organisations like the Education Foundation, and we’d love to boost funds for those,” Nick said.

While the truck parade promises to be the showstopper, attendees can expect a full day of activities at the showground, including a show and shine competition, raffles, market stalls, historic vehicles and engines, live music and children’s activities.

The idea for the festival originally came to Nick after he entered several of his trucks in Goulburn’s Convoy for Kids.

“I just thought that we could do something like that in Braidwood, and it grew from there,” Nick said.

A full closure of Wallace Street is required to manage the truck convoy. Photo: The Braidwood Big Wheels Festival.

Nick spent the past few years arranging permits and road closures to ensure the big day goes off without a hitch, and he was determined not to take no for an answer.

“We had a little grief trying to get the parade through town,” Nick said.

“We were basically told that the only thing that shuts the main street of Braidwood is the ANZAC Day parade.”

With the Wallace Street road closure secured after plenty of persistence, Nick reflected on why he believes the festival will resonate with people and attract a crowd.

“Trucks are a part of Australian life, especially in regional Australia; without them, and having no train links out here, we’d be in a bit of strife,” he said.

As the man responsible for transporting the grog to Braidwood and Captains Flat, Nick plays a key role, and possibly the most important logistics role, in the region. He’s looking forward to sharing his enthusiasm for trucks with the wider community.

“People get quite passionate about their trucks, keeping them neat and tidy.”

Given the level of planning and preparation involved, Nick is reluctant to promise that the event will become an annual tradition if it proves successful. However, he hopes it could become a biennial event the town can look forward to.

For more information on the Big Wheels Festival, head to the website.

Original Article published by Tenele Conway on About Regional.

canberra.title: Australian Wine List of the Year awards raise a glass (or three) to great hospitality
canberra.snippet: More than 300 of the hospitality and wine industry’s finest gathered to celebrate the 33rd Australian Wine List of the Year Awards recent...
canberra.content:
3 October 2026

Start the conversation

Louis Sheffield and Kate Hibberson from The Boat House at the Australian Wine List of the Year Awards. Photo: Supplied.

More than 300 of the hospitality and wine industry’s finest gathered to celebrate the 33rd Australian Wine List of the Year Awards recently in Sydney.

The awards are the national bench mark for excellent wine lists in restaurants and bars and the ACT was once again well represented.

The Boat House is no stranger to these awards. Last year it was inducted into the Hall of Fame for its consistent excellence and this year it was again awarded the title of Best Wine List ACT.

Sommelier Kate Hibberson has been running the wine program at The Boat House for many years but has been training young mentee Louis Sheffield, who has stepped into the spotlight.

He started out pouring beers at Bentspoke, but fell in love with wine and has been steadily training and getting more experience.

“I’ve been learning on the job from Kate over the last two and half years, as well as doing a few education courses. I’ve now taken the next leap and I’m starting to put my own impression on the wine program here,” Louis told Region.

“My aim is always to make it more accessible for both staff and customers. I want choosing a wine to be an approachable, enjoyable and educational experience for everyone.”

The judges described The Boat House’s wine list as “a short, sharp list that’s loaded with liquid enticements”.

Capitol Bar & Grill at QT Canberra celebrated a hat-trick, winning the award for Australia’s Best Listing of ACT and Canberra District Wines for the third year running. Judges noted the breadth of its list, which incorporates many local producers from across the region.

Rizla won the national award for Best Wine List (under 100 wines) in 2025 and was a finalist this year. Photo: Supplied.

Braddon’s Riesling bar Rizla was a finalist for Australia’s Best Wine List (Max 100 Wines); a hotly contested category which it won last year.

Venues on the list receive a rating of one, two or three “glasses” (or “stems”), indicating that their wine list is recommended, excellent or outstanding.

For Louis, this award is a recognition of not only their own hard work at The Boat House, but a broader celebration of the local hospitality community.

“It allows us to showcase the Canberra district and how far Canberra hospitality and wineries have come. We have such a knowledgeable, understanding customer base full of people who want to try new things and explore what’s growing around them.

“It means the most that a lot of the wine producers we work with reached out to congratulate me. It feels good to put their stuff forward to say ‘we’re proud of you and here’s how your wine stacks up’.”

Louis is planning to start a Diploma in Wines through the Wine and Spirits Education Trust and hopes to share his new skills to the rest of The Boat House staff.

Results for ACT venues:

Australia’s Best Listing of ACT and Canberra District Wines: Capital Bar & Grill
Best Wine List ACT: The Boat House

Three glasses:

The Boat House
Rizla
Romanée Wine Bar
Raku Dining

Two glasses:

Bar Outro
Beltana Farm
Chairman & Yip
Capitol Bar and Grill
Les Bistronomes
Lunetta

canberra.title: Rosa’s walks into a bright future with the reopening of the National Rose Gardens
canberra.snippet: Rosa’s at The Lawns is entering a new era, and there couldn’t be a better season for a fresh start than spring, with its pavilion-s...
canberra.content:
Rosa’s at The Lawns has made it through a tough 18 months and has entered a new chapter in time for spring. Photo: Rosa’s.

Rosa’s at The Lawns is entering a new era, and there couldn’t be a better season for a fresh start than spring, with its pavilion-style dining spilling out onto one of Canberra’s best terraces, making it one of the capital’s premier all-day dining destinations.

The fresh outlook comes with the reopening of the National Rose Gardens that sit on Rosa’s doorstep. In a case of spectacularly bad timing, the rose gardens have been under lengthy construction behind a 2.2 metre-tall perimeter fence, overshadowing Rosa’s garden outlook.

With the 18-month project finally complete, director of operations Amber Maddigan can look back on the difficult period with the clarity of hindsight and feels a full closure may have been a better direction for the business, with the fencing deterring clientele, many of whom thought they were closed.

“It should have been the year we built on everything we’d learnt in our first, but instead we found ourselves operating at a significant loss just to keep our team employed, while still being there for our regulars,” Amber says.

“We thought maintaining momentum would see us come out the other end firing, but in hindsight, with the delays, we would have been better off if we had closed.”

Rosa’s sits on the edge of the refurbished National Rose Gardens with its pavilion-style dining spilling into the terrace. Photo: Rosa’s.

With spring officially hitting the region with the opening of Floriade, Amber and her team have refocused on what Rosa’s can become in its iconic location.

“Our vision has always been bigger than simply operating a hospitality venue. We want this to be a place where locals and visitors come together to gather, celebrate and enjoy this incredibly special part of the National Capital,” Amber tells Region.

“In many ways, it’s about bringing the precinct back to what it was created to be when it was first built in 1968: a place for people. It’s a special part of the capital, and we feel a huge sense of responsibility to deliver on that.”

Rosa’s heads into spring with a breakfast menu that’s available from Wednesday until Sunday. Photo: Rosa’s.

Best remembered as the Lobby Restaurant, the renowned building has found new life as Rosa’s. Her postmodernist aesthetic suits a space designed to open to the elements, letting diners feel part of the rose gardens bordering its expansive windows and terrace.

It feels like a step into a new future and a nod to the past all at once, and the enthusiasm among the returning patrons is palpable.

“This spring and summer feels like a new chapter for us. The gardens are back in view and better than ever, the precinct is opening up again, and we can finally have a proper go at delivering that vision,” Amber says.

“We’re excited to see people back on the lawns and this iconic part of the National Triangle full of life again.”

Not to let the stunning gardens outdo the menu, Rosa’s has launched a breakfast menu from Wednesdays until Sundays from 7 am. Healthy options such as smashed avocado on toasted sourdough with stracciatella and heirloom tomatoes sit alongside indulgences including brioche French toast with whipped ricotta and pistachio cream.

Rosa’s is well known for its wood-fired pizza menu. Photo: Rosa’s.

Breakfast seamlessly rolls into lunchtime, where Canberra’s glorious weather meets antipasto, pizzas and cocktails, and from 7 October, dinner will also be available 5 nights a week from Wednesday until Sunday.

While families enjoying the park-like gardens are understandably drawn to the wood-fired pizzas, it’s the grazing dishes that bring a leisurely afternoon at Rosa’s to life.

The smoked pork terrine with zuni pickled onions and caperberries is a wonderful sharing starter. Photo: Martin Conway.

The braised lamb meatballs are atop a lovely soft polenta and covered in a tomato sugo sauce. Photo: Martin Conway.

The salmon en papillote comes with capers, olives,fennel, zucchini and pomodoro. Photo: Martin Conway.

The ricotta gnocchi is served with stracciatelli, salsa verde and a rich creamy vodka sauce. Photo: Martin Conway.

Wood-fired puffed bread served with olive oil and aged balsamic provides the ideal anchor for sharing dishes like the smoky baba ganoush, a wonderfully savoury smoked pork terrine sharpened by tart pickled accompaniments, and plump, succulent lamb meatballs nestled on soft polenta.

The grazing plates are joined by more substantial dishes, including pillowy ricotta gnocchi in a creamy vodka sauce, topped with a crunchy pangratatta. For something heartier, there’s sirloin steak or salmon en papillote with capers, olives, fennel, zucchini and pomodoro.

Mains can and should be followed by dessert, with the tiramisu proving particularly delightful.

The drinks list is thoughtfully designed to move with diners through the day. Breakfast cocktails offer a cheeky start, while local and interstate wines sit alongside Canberra favourites BentSpoke and Capital Brewing Co on tap.

With loads of outdoor space, the whole family will love Rosa’s. Photo: Rosa’s.

With all-day dining now in full swing and the gardens looking better than ever, diners who are taken with Rosa’s, as they likely will be, can now book the space for weddings and private events, rounding out the offering at this landmark venue that has a bright future.

“There’s a real sense of momentum returning. Christmas party bookings are up, we’ve got a great line-up of events, promotions and live music planned, and over the coming months I think people are going to see the precinct really come to life.”

Rosa’s is located at 7 King George Terrace, Parkes. From 7 October until 3 April, Rosa’s will operate extended summer hours, opening from 7 am to 8 pm on Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Sundays, and until late on Fridays and Saturdays.

canberra.title: Bogong ‘miracle’ a reason to cheer
canberra.snippet: I think anyone in Canberra with an interest in the natural world is well aware that something seemingly miraculous is happening all aroun...
canberra.content:
A wall of Bogong moths, aestivating in a cave in the Australian Alps. Photo: Professor Eric Warrant.

I think anyone in Canberra with an interest in the natural world is well aware that something seemingly miraculous is happening all around us right now.

Vast numbers of the lovely grey-patterned Bogong Moths have returned on their annual trip south, as they had for millennia until just a few years ago when the apparently infinite stream of them suddenly dried up.

This began in 2017 at the start of the savage drought that lasted until about 2020. There was serious concern for their future, but now, after a few wet years, they have bounced back.

Bogongs are a direct link to a colder Australia, which began to warm again with the end of the last glaciation period, some 10,000 years ago. For a long time before that, most of eastern Australia was similar to the highlands of the southern mountains today – cold, windy and mostly treeless – and that suited the Bogongs well.

Today the Bogongs breed on the black soil plains of northern NSW and southern Queensland. The caterpillars – known to unappreciative farmers as ‘cut worms’ – shelter underground by day and emerge at night to feed on pasture plants, substitutes for the native herbage they used to rely on.

In spring, as temperatures rise, they pupate, emerge as moths and fly south, travelling by night and feeding on eucalypt nectar. They navigate by the stars, using a map hard-wired into their minute brains.

Unlike migratory birds, they can’t follow older, experienced individuals, as no Bogong ever makes the trip twice.

When they get to the mountains, they head to the same rock shelters in Namadgi, Kosciuszko and the Victorian Alps that thousands of generations of their foremoths have used before them. The first arrivals get the deepest, coolest crevices, and later arrivals tuck their heads under the wings of the moths already there, a tiled wall of moths at a density of over 15,000 per square metre.

In the mountains, they don’t feed, but every night clouds of them emerge like smoke from the rocks and return by dawn. We might think it’s to escape the Mountain Pygmy Possums and other small native mammals that snack at night on their rich, fatty bodies, but it’s really a no-win for them, as in the air they’re hunted by Boobook Owls, bats and Owlet-nightjars. So why do they do it? Only the moths know, and they’re not telling.

Little Ravens in the cloud on Mount Kosciuszko, searching the crevices for accessible Bogongs. Photo: Ian Fraser.

Another, equally dangerous and far more insidious predator of the moths exists. Two species of tiny parasitic mermithid roundworms have adapted entirely to the Bogong migration. They overwinter as eggs on the cave floor and in spring they swim up the walls in melting snow water and infect the arriving moths as they drink the water. In January they leave the dying hosts and return to the floor, rich in moth bodies and debris, to mature, mate and leave eggs to await next year’s moths.

In late summer the Bogongs fly north again, lay eggs and then they all die, leaving the next generation in the black soil to carry on.

The numbers are phenomenal. It is reported that a Sydney church service was interrupted in 1865 while the congregation was counting 80,000 moths on the windows. I’m not sure how that lack of concentration was the moths’ fault, though!

Their preferred route is usually the more direct inland one, but they are at the mercy of the winds too and often turn up at the coast, as they are this year.

At times, clouds of moths have even been blown across the Tasman and arrived in New Zealand.

Bogong Moth tastefully settled on a doormat. Photo: Ian Fraser.

The great and sadly late CSIRO moth expert Ted Edwards once described our Parliament House as the world’s biggest moth trap, and so it proved when vast numbers of moths were distracted by the overnight lights and then took refuge in the house when daylight came. This was not at all where they wanted to be, but certain under-informed members then insulted them by accusing them of being a threat to the great house tapestries! These moths eat only nectar. It was sort of funny at the time, but probably not so much for the moths.

I, for one, am in dire need of some good news stories these days, and the return of the Bogongs has given me great cheer.

Ian Fraser is a Canberra naturalist, conservationist and author. He has written on all aspects of natural history, advised the ACT Government on biodiversity and published multiple guides to the region’s flora and fauna.

canberra.title: Galilee School unveils garden to recognise collective effort behind 25-year journey
canberra.snippet: Galilee School has created a Commemorative Garden at its Kambah campus to honour the contributors who have helped the special assistance ...
canberra.content:
3 October 2026

Start the conversation

Galilee School principal Tim McNevin (front) with inaugural inductees to the Galilee School Commemorative Garden – Craig Webber, Robert Long and Paul Adcock. Photo: Supplied.

Galilee School has created a Commemorative Garden at its Kambah campus to honour the contributors who have helped the special assistance school over the past 25 years.

The legacy project recognises the people and organisations that helped shape the school since it launched in 1999 and will be maintained by students.

The idea was raised during the school’s 25th anniversary celebrations in 2025 and was pitched as a place for students, staff, families, alumni, supporters and the wider school community to reflect on and recognise the values of the school.

The garden features native plants, stonework, pathways and commemorative markers including the spiral garden, which honours those who have contributed to the school’s growth and its impact on the lives of hundreds of young people.

Principal Tim McNevin said the garden reflected the collective effort behind the school’s journey.

“The Commemorative Garden is more than a tribute to our past. It is a recognition that Galilee School exists today because of the vision, determination and generosity of countless people who believed that every young person deserves the opportunity to succeed,” he said.

“This garden ensures their contribution is remembered and celebrated for generations to come.

“Galilee School supports young people who have experienced significant barriers to mainstream education, through individualised learning, wellbeing support and practical pathways for the future.”

The inaugural inductees represent people and organisations whose contributions have had a lasting impact on the school’s development, culture and success, with more to be recognised in future years.

The garden also commemorates significant milestone events in the life of the school, including the devastating 2003 Canberra bushfires that effectively destroyed the Kambah campus.

Communities at Work Board chair Trixie Makay said the garden created an important link between the school’s history and its future.

“We are proud to recognise the remarkable individuals and organisations whose leadership, advocacy and support have helped Galilee School create opportunities for young people who have experienced significant barriers to education.

“The garden creates a lasting place of acknowledgement and appreciation, connecting past and present generations of the Galilee School community.”

Visit Galilee School to learn more about its work.

australia.title: Five-year-old girl in critical condition after car hits crowd in Newcastle
australia.snippet: P-plate driver arrested at scene after vehicle strikes Knights fans attending grand final farewell, leaving 10 injured including three ch...
australia.content:
Ten people have been injured, one critically, after a car crashed into a crowd of people in Newcastle waiting to farewell the Knights team bus before the NRL grand final.

New South Wales police said a five-year-old girl remained in a critical condition after the crash on Saturday morning.

Initially a 67-year-old man was also in a critical. The man is now in a serious but stable condition.

John Hunter hospital provided an update to Australian Associated Press on Saturday night confirming five other patients were in a stable condition and three others had been discharged.

The injured were treated on the scene by NSW ambulance paramedics, before being taken to hospital.

The P-plate driver was an 18-year-old man who was arrested at the scene and taken to hospital for mandatory testing, police said.

The assistant commissioner David Waddell said there were reports the man was driving erratically before losing control and careening into the crowd. It was expected he would be charged later on Saturday.

The man had two others in the car with him.

“We had to get them out of there because the crowd did turn on them,” Waddell said.

The police minister, Yasmin Catley, said so many lives had been affected by a split-second decision, as she urged other drivers to take care over the NSW long weekend.

“We have already started Saturday morning with this devastation,” she said.

“Nobody can comprehend what has happened with this terrible tragedy.”

The roads minister, Jenny Aitchison, said the incident could have been worse, with more than 1,000 people gathered in the area where it occurred.

Emergency services were called to Newcastle Link Road at the Transfield Drive roundabout in Wallsend about 9.30am on Saturday after reports a vehicle struck multiple people in a crowd.

“Several people have been injured and are currently receiving treatment at the scene,” police said.

“Police have commenced an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident, with initial inquiries indicating it is not believed to be terror related.”

Gavin Morris, the mayor of Newcastle, told the ABC that the driver, who he said was a Knights fan, lost control while revving his car shortly before the team arrived.

“I’ve spoken to the authorities, a number of which, and look, first of all, it is under investigation, and the young driver is now with police, so it appears that he was revving the car in some form. He was excited. He was a supporter. He was, you know, a fan,” Morris said.

“It appears that he’s lost control of the car, and he’s gone … sideways into the crowd.”

Footage posted on social media appeared to show the car being driven quickly around a roundabout shortly before the crash.

Other images showed it had careened off the road soon afterwards.

A witness to the incident, Dylan Prior told ABC News that the car was “revving a bit” before it ran into a group of people.

“I saw some young kids go flying, and people running to help the victims,” he said.

“Everyone was yelling and hysterical, yelling at the driver.

“They were screaming for help.”

The Newcastle Link Road was closed in both directions, leading to the diversion of the Knights grand final procession.

The club confirmed in an Instagram post that it had changed its route, apologising to fans who may have missed farewelling the team but saying “public safety is our priority”.

Police appealed for fans to leave the area.

“Police acknowledge many loyal supporters may have missed the opportunity to see the team and show their support.

“Members of the public are asked to safely disperse from the area and keep roadways clear to assist emergency services and traffic management efforts.

“Police thank the community for their patience, cooperation and assistance.”

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, said his thoughts were with the families and friends of those injured.

“It’s heartbreaking to see fans who were sending off their grand final team involved in such a terrible incident,” he said.

“We’ve seen how this grand final has brought Newcastle together, and I hope the whole community remains united as we continue to respond.”

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said he had spoken with Minns and offered the federal government’s support.

“My thoughts are with everyone injured or involved in the horrible incident this morning in Newcastle,” Albanese said in a statement.

“I want to acknowledge and thank emergency services and police for responding so quickly, and their ongoing work in treating the injured.

“Rugby league brings people together, and this should have been a weekend of excitement and pride for Newcastle fans.”

- Australian Associated Press contributed to this report

australia.title: One Nation vows to abolish First Nations treaty and legalise pepper spray at Victorian campaign launch
australia.snippet: Candidate Mark Nicholson said former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan would be ‘in prison by Christmas’ if One Nation won the el...
australia.content:
One Nation has launched its Victorian election campaign, vowing to legalise the personal use of pepper spray, abolish the state’s treaty with Indigenous people, and scrap payroll tax in regional Victoria.

A social media post announcing its policy to “make it cheaper and easier to set up new businesses in Victoria” featured an AI-generated image of a “taaditional [sic] fish n’chips” shop.

One Nation used its official campaign launch at Crown Casino to unveil candidates for the state’s upper house and all 88 lower house electorates.

These candidates include a former Liberal who has won support from alleged underworld figures, a naturopath who has endorsed Donald Trump’s unfounded claim that paracetamol is linked to autism and a former shire councillor who lost his licence for drink-driving.

The party is understood to have again prevented reporters from certain media outlets from attending the launch. It has previously barred the ABC, Guardian, and the Age from its media events. The Guardian did not attempt to attend Saturday’s launch.

The Herald Sun reported that Northern Metropolitan candidate and creator of the party’s Please Explain Cartoon, Mark Nicholson, vowed at the launch that if One Nation won the election, former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan would be “in prison by Christmas”.

Details of other policies were scant online, but a 63-page document was reportedly circulated at the event that included plans to “gang up on gangs”.

Images of the document show it was described as One Nation’s policy platform and “The Real Deal for Victoria”, with a focus on restoring safety, prosperity and trust.

According to the party’s website on Saturday afternoon, an “update [was] in progress” regarding its crime policy.

The party’s Victorian state president, Warren Pickering, told radio 3AW Melbourne on Friday that crime and bail remained a top priority for One Nation.

“[It] is the key issue in the state right now and people need to feel safe in their homes and places of work once more,” he said.

“You make that happen by taking a pragmatic approach, not an expensive one, to ensuring we get more police on the streets, get our empty stations manned and ensure bail laws and sentences are fitting with the crimes.”

The party claimed in social media posts that more than 1,000 people attended the launch, but other estimates put the crowd at several hundred lower than that. A smaller group of protesters outside were monitored by police.

The party has come under fire for practices that could see it collect as much as $633,000 from people who have nominated for the Victorian election, with some potential candidates questioning whether the party is staging a “cash grab”.

While the party has fashioned itself as representing the working class, its founder Pauline Hanson has faced a series of revelations about her links to billionaire Gina Rinehart, including exclusive use of a private jet, and staying at her multimillion-dollar homes.

– Additional reporting by Australian Associated Press

australia.title: Flood watch for most of Victoria as heavy rain continues, with storms forecast in parts of NSW
australia.snippet: BoM expects falls of up to 90mm in parts of Victoria as severe weather system continues to sweep the southern states A severe weather sys...
australia.content:
A severe weather system continues to dump heavy rain into sodden riverine catchments across Victoria, sparking widespread warnings of transport disruption and delays.

The Bureau of Meteorology has issued a flood watch for most of Victoria including the north-east, central, south-west and north-west, as well as parts of Gippsland.

It also said bursts of heavy rain accompanied by potentially damaging winds and thunderstorms were possible in parts of New South Wales as a band of heavy weather swept the southern states.

In Victoria, the Otway Ranges, south-west of Melbourne, and Gippsland are facing 24-hour rain totals up to 90mm, with isolated falls up to 150mm possible in elevated regions.

Six-hourly totals up to 70mm have been forecast, with conditions not expected to ease until late Saturday.

Gippsland is also likely to be hard hit, with 24-hour totals between 50 and 80mm likely and isolated falls up to 110mm possible, with conditions easing Sunday morning.

“This is on top of the rain you’ve already had in the last few days, so I’ll say it again, the soils are already saturated,” senior meteorologist Angus Hines said.

Over 100mm has already fallen in parts of the Otways, with heavy rain continuing to fall on Saturday afternoon.

“Another 30 to 50mm on top of last night’s deluge could certainly fall there,” Hines said.

The rain was centred around a low pressure system situated over the Murray River on the NSW-Victorian border.

For now, there was just one official flood warning in place for the Bunyip River in Victoria but Hines said more rivers were likely to see rises across the weekend.

He said the situation was dynamic and it was highly likely more flood warnings would be issued.

In NSW, a severe thunderstorm warning has been issued for the Illawarra and parts of south coast, central and southern tablelands, the central west slopes and plains.

Locations which may be affected include Orange, Goulburn, Dubbo, Nowra, Bowral and Bathurst.

The severe weather is expected to clear by the end of the weekend.

australia.title: OpenAI says its review into hacks, including on Australian government sites, is costing $500,000 a day
australia.snippet: Company says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisation Get our bre...
australia.content:
OpenAI says its review in response to the Medicare and Hugging Face agent attacks is costing the company more than US$500,000 per day, as it deploys AI to examine data that would take a human 66m years to read.

The company has warned the review is ongoing, and more organisations may be informed they’ve been targeted in the near future.

On Friday evening, OpenAI revealed agents had hacked into a New South Wales government website in June and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.

It is the sixth government website in Australia to be notified by the AI giant since last month of agent activity on their services, after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announced OpenAI’s agents had hacked into Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal.

The reason for the delay compared to the revelation of the Medicare attack is due to the sheer volume of data OpenAI needs to review.

In a blog post this week the company revealed the large amount of work involved in reviewing its agents’ activity.

OpenAI said it has to review 50 petabytes of data – roughly 50m gigabytes.

“We’re working back through the records month by month, looking for potential unintended activity beyond the cases we’ve already found,” the company said.

“To put that in perspective, if that were all plain English text, it would take one person about 66 million years to read it at 240 words a minute, reading nonstop without ever sleeping or taking a break.”

The company is searching records for where models accessed and changed websites, or took actions involving passwords, application programming interface (API) access or other sensitive credentials.

AI is being used to help sift through the records, and it was costing the company more than half a million US dollars per day to go through. OpenAI said it also plans to increase its computing power as the process is refined.

As of late last month, more than 100 organisations had been notified of having being targeted by OpenAI’s agents, but the company said notifying an organisation does not mean private information was accessed or that their system was compromised.

OpenAI said it expects to find more cases and notify more organisations about events that may have occurred months ago.

Organisations will be informed privately if they need to investigate and address potential security issues, and OpenAI has said it will publicly report findings about agent behaviour and identified weaknesses in safeguards for the broader AI sector.

“We err on the side of notification when our models’ activity exposes a potential security vulnerability, even in cases where it is unclear if the information accessed was intended to be public, so the organization can investigate and take appropriate action,” OpenAI said.

OpenAI discovered the latest NSW government website breach on Tuesday, and informed the state government and the Australian Signals Directorate after a 48-hour review.

The Medicare breach has prompted the Australian government to require departments and agencies to undertake a stocktake of legacy technology to reduce the number of ageing systems within government and reduce the cybersecurity risk they may present in the event of an AI agent attack.

Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google will front a joint parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence in Sydney on Tuesday.

australia.title: Magnitude 4.8 earthquake hits Victoria with tremors felt across Melbourne
australia.snippet: The epicentre was at Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with residents reporting houses shaking just after 2am Get our breaking ne...
australia.content:
A magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck Victoria in the early hours of Saturday morning, shaking Melbourne and waking people across the whole region.

Geoscience Australia said it detected an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8 at 2.01am near Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with the tremors felt across the city’s eastern suburbs.

Geoscience Australia said it had received thousands of reports from people who said they had felt the earthquake.

Posting on Facebook, Brian Morley in Narre Warren said “felt it and woke me up”, while Theresa Stevens said: “Shook our house in Garfield.”

Other posts indicated the quake had been felt in Preston, Heidelberg Heights, Venus Bay and many other parts of Melbourne.

The quake was estimated to have struck at about 10km below the Earth’s surface.

Victoria’s State Emergency Service said the earthquake was a “timely reminder” to remember the drill to follow during an earthquake and that was drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy piece of furniture and protect your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.

The Bureau of Meteorology said there was no tsunami threat from the quake.

The quake occurred in a region of South Gippsland considered to be amongst the most active seismic zones in Australia.

Victoria’s two most recent quakes with magnitudes of 5 or above, however, were recorded elsewhere: a 5.9 magnitude in 2021 near Mansfield, in the state’s north-east, and a 5.0 on the Great Ocean Road in 2023.

The quake on Saturday morning was the largest recorded in the state since that shock in 2023.

An aftershock of 3.1 magnitude was recorded 55 minutes after the 4.8 magnitude earthquake early Saturday, with a magnitude 3.3 earthquake also recorded on Thursday morning at Yarram, about 80km east of Leongatha.

Mark Quigley, associate professor of earthquake science at the University of Melbourne, said aftershocks could be felt for weeks in the region.

“South Gippsland is one of our more seismically active parts of the country,” Quigley told the ABC.

“We know it’s an area where seismicity is common, [and] we know we would expect aftershocks from an earthquake of that magnitude.”

He said the earthquake was the result of a two by three kilometre area of rock about 10km below the surface slipping five to 10 cm rapidly, releasing seismic energy.

Quigley said that earthquakes were not being recorded more often, despite a seeming increase in frequency in recent years.

While the earthquake was “not an opportunity for people to panic or anything”, Quigley said it could be useful for people who lived in the region to consider whether they had items in their houses that could be damaged or create a safety risk in the event of a larger quake.

“We know from the geological record we’ve had much larger in Gippsland in the past, larger than six and possibly as large as magnitude seven which I can assure you would cause widespread damage should they occur.”

The last earthquake to cause property damage in Victoria was the 2021 quake, which resulted in tremors about 700km from the epicentre.

world.title: Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities
world.snippet: Western Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks down Allegations that the son of the Liby...
world.content:
Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in western Libya have upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country.

Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.

But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.

Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors.

Donald Trump’s Africa adviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister.

Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.”

But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces.

Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.

On 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar.

Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said.

The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change.

Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.”

He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war.

The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east.

Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance.

world.title: Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin
world.snippet: Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric cla...
world.content:
On the eve of the Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.

Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by a group of young volunteers, Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.

But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the 14th-century BCE pharaoh’s origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.

Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.

The team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.

Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.

“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.

“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”

Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.

One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.

Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.

“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.

“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.

This is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, a Netflix documentary provoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedly gave an Afrocentric perspective of Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.

Monica Hanna, a prominent Egyptologist and assistant professor of archaeology at the American University of Iraq–Baghdad, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.

“Egyptians were never one skin colour,” she said. “We are not snow-white, or the colour of cream.”

Walid Mahmoud, an AI researcher and expert in African anthropology, said AI tools such as ChatGPT reflected whatever information was most widely shared online, rather than what was factually accurate.

They were built by companies in the US and Europe, he said, and the content they generated could shape how those audiences saw themselves.

“That’s why we should never simply accept what it produces, especially when it comes to cultural identity and heritage,” Mahmoud said.

Mostafa Eissa, an art critic, said AI should remain a tool, never a decision-maker in its own right.

“I favour using technology without abandoning the human element within the artist,” he said, warning that letting such tools substitute an artist’s own skill risked emptying a work of its originality.

  • This article is published in collaboration with Egab

world.title: Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad
world.snippet: Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rights With hours left befor...
world.content:
With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.

On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use.

Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF).

Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa.

“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”

The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, immigration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.

“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.

“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”

A Democratic congressional aide said Shaheen had maintained 10 holds on $22m of awards focusing on Brazil, South Africa, Nigeria, and the promotion of a rightwing ideology in the United Kingdom and in Europe. According to the aide, secretary of state Marco Rubio had personally signed a memo to disregard the holds and obligate the funds.

The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.

In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).

Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.

The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”.

“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe, which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”

Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse.

The Guardian first reported that Trump officials had drawn up no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe. ProPublica similarly reported that there were at least a dozen no-bid grants earmarked for rightwing projects.

The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.

A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.

A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.

One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.

And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.

The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).

The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and enforced by Ofcom, it has age-verification rules – which took effect last year – that have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship.

The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News.

The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, regarding issues including online safety law to immigration.

world.title: South African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killings
world.snippet: President announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of women South Africa’s president has called on men to take mo...
world.content:
South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders.

Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days.

In a televised speech on Tuesday night, the president said local governments would have five months to address issues that compromised women’s safety, from broken streetlights to overgrown public spaces and abandoned buildings. He added that he had tasked five ministers to come up with a plan within 60 days to reduce alcohol-fuelled violence.

“Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator,” Ramaphosa said. “But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort.

“Women should not have to live in fear because government has failed to repair a light, clear a public space, process evidence or enforce a law.”

South Africa has been gripped by grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Eight of the women were found in the last three weeks, including Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who was discovered on 12 September after she went missing when she went for a run after work.

Ramaphosa said suspects had been arrested in connection with three of the killings and that the other cases would not be left to go cold. He added that police had not found evidence that a serial killer was responsible for all 11 killings, but that all possibilities were still being investigated.

He directly addressed South African men, urging them to challenge relatives, friends and colleagues who harassed, humiliated or abused women. “It is time for good men to stop being silent men,” he said.

“For too long, gender-based violence has been treated as a woman’s problem to solve. Women march, the women of our country organise, they speak out, they protest, they confront and they comfort survivors,” Ramaphosa said.

“Women change their routes home. Avoid going out at night and warn one another about dangerous places and dangerous men. We have placed the burden of male violence on women. That must change.”

Activists expressed their frustration that solid policy actions had not been taken years ago and scepticism that the measures Ramaphosa had announced would work.

Shenilla Mohamed, the executive director of Amnesty International South Africa, said: “These are not new issues and as a country we have been talking about ways to tackle the high numbers of [gender-based violence and femicide], especially since 2019 when women took to the streets to protest, and yet here we are again in the face of continued attacks against women.

“Amnesty International South Africa also notes the timelines put in place by the president, but this will only mean something if it results in action, and if there are consequences for inaction.”

Mpiwa Mangwiro-Tsanga and Bafana Khumalo, of Sonke Gender Justice, an NGO, said: “Our concern … is that the response remains heavily weighted towards what happens after violence has already occurred.”

They added: “Investigating unresolved cases, processing forensic evidence and repairing unsafe public spaces are necessary, but they do not constitute a comprehensive prevention strategy. It is concerning that the president is asking municipalities to do what is actually their mandate and yet they do not deliver on these.”

world.title: Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US
world.snippet: Burundi joins several other African nations in accepting people deported under Trump’s hardline policy Burundi has agreed to join a clutc...
world.content:
Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of ⁠other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under ⁠Donald Trump’s hardline ⁠immigration ​policy.

However, Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said ⁠Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial ⁠details.

Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to about half ​a dozen African nations ‌as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals ‌that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of ‌dollars.

In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.

Mutoni said preparations were under way to arrange accommodation, ‌living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they ​will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.

“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law ⁠will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.

Burundi aimed ​to both ​strengthen diplomatic relations and provide ​hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson ​added.

The US ‌state department ​did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.
